title: Commentary on the Gospel of Luke
subtitle: Selected homilies on the Annunciation, Nativity, Theophany, and Transfiguration
source: Summarized from the translation of the Syriac by R. Payne Smith (Oxford, 1859), public domain. Editorial framing and notes by the editors of Purify.

sections.title: The Annunciation: 'Hail, full of grace'
paragraphs: Cyril begins the Lukan commentary at the door at which the whole economy of salvation enters: the angel's greeting to the Virgin. He notes that the salutation is not the form ordinary among the Hebrews. The angel does not say 'Peace be with you'; he says 'Hail, full of grace; the Lord is with you'. The greeting is the prophecy. The grace which is now to be poured out on the world is already, by anticipation, present in her.

Cyril dwells on the Virgin's question, 'How shall this be, since I know not a man?' This is not unbelief, he says, as Zechariah's question to the same angel had been. It is the question of one who is told something contrary to the order of nature and seeks to know in what manner God will act. The angel answers her, and her answer to the angel is the consent on which the Incarnation hinges: 'Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word.'
notes: The text comes from R. Payne Smith's translation of the Syriac, since the Greek of the Commentary on Luke survives only in fragments. The Syriac version preserves the bulk of the work in continuous form.
Cyril's reading of the Annunciation became the foundation of the Eastern Marian troparia at the Annunciation feast on March 25, and at the eves of the Nativity and Theophany.

sections.title: The Nativity: 'Today in the city of David'
paragraphs: Cyril takes up the Nativity narrative as a sustained meditation on the union of God and man. The angels sing 'Glory to God in the highest and on earth peace among men of His good pleasure' precisely because the One who is born is God Himself, descending into our nature. The peace announced is not a peace between nations; it is the peace of God reconciled to humanity in the Person of His Son.

Cyril is careful to note that the swaddling bands are real swaddling bands and the manger a real manger. The Word does not seem to be born; He is born. The infancy is His infancy. The hunger and weariness and growth in wisdom and stature attributed to the Child in Luke are the proper experiences of the incarnate Word, who did not despise to be carried at His mother's breast.
notes: Cyril uses the Nativity homilies to refute the Apollinarian residue in his own day: any teaching that the Word took only a part of human nature, or replaced the rational soul with the divinity. He insists on a full and complete human nature, body and rational soul, assumed by the Word.
The homilies on the Nativity, the Circumcision, and the Presentation are read in the Eastern Office on the corresponding feasts; selections appear in the liturgical lectionaries to this day.

sections.title: The Baptism in the Jordan: the Theophany
paragraphs: Cyril reads the Baptism not as the moment when the Word came down upon Jesus, as some Gnostics taught, but as the public revelation of who Jesus already was. The voice from heaven, 'This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased', does not give a status that was not there before; it reveals to John and to the crowds and to us the eternal sonship of the One who stands in the river.

Cyril dwells on why the One who needed no cleansing came to be baptized. The answer is the answer of the Fathers before him: He came to sanctify the waters, so that those who would be baptized into His name might come up from the same Jordan into the same sonship. He took the place of the sinner so that the sinner might take, by grace, the place of the Son.
notes: The Eastern feast of Theophany on January 6 celebrates this revelation of the Trinity at the Jordan, and the homily Cyril gives in this section is read in part at the Great Blessing of the Waters.
Cyril's reading is anti-Adoptionist: nothing happens to Christ at His Baptism that He was not already eternally. What happens is revelation, not promotion.

sections.title: The Transfiguration on Tabor
paragraphs: Cyril treats the Transfiguration as the central revelation of the unity of natures in Christ. Peter and James and John see, with bodily eyes, the divinity of the One they have walked with as a man. The light that shines from Him is not a light borrowed from elsewhere; it is the light that He has always had, made visible to His disciples as their eyes are made able to bear it.

Cyril insists that the same Person is glorified and was hungry; the same Christ who is seen on the mountain in light is the one who weeps at the tomb of Lazarus. The Transfiguration is the showing of what He always is, given to the disciples that they may stand under the Cross and not despair.
notes: Cyril's reading of Tabor as the unveiling of the divine glory eternally proper to Christ is the patristic ground on which St. Gregory Palamas will later build the doctrine of the uncreated energies.
The Eastern feast of the Transfiguration on August 6 keeps Cyril's homily in its lectionary tradition; the kontakion of the feast speaks the same theology in compressed liturgical form.
